Bon*Bön*German{}|Etymology}Borrowed bo.|Noun}from German noun}#&_
^ö*Bonhase*German{}|Alternative forms}Böhnhase|Etymology}From Middle Low German bönhase,from Middle Low German tcat,from Middle Low German tloft,attic+from Middle Low German thare,the former being cognate of from German tstage. The word is first attested in the early 14th century as a personal name (and is thus probably even older). Since the 15th century it meant “illegally working craftsperson”. The sense “cat” is only attested later on,but there can be little doubt that it is the original meaning. Compare from German Dachhase,from English roof rabbit,etc.,which in fact must be loan translations of the Low German unless there were some ancient source for all of them. It was formerly supposed that the illegal workers were called  as a pun on from Ancient Greek tworker in an ignoble trade,whence later from German Banause,but this is highly unlikely since Greek studies were only just being revived in the 15th century. More probably these workers were simply compared to stray cats who holed up in lofts and fled when chased (as they commonly were by the members of the official guilds).|Pronunciation}/ˈbøːnˌhaːzə/}^Ⓓ1/14/De-^@.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#North Germany cat; roof rabbit}•synononym:Dachhase}#North Germany A skilled manual worker or craftsperson who works illegally,originally without the concession of the respective guild.}#North Germany botcher; bungler Literally:[incompetent worker]}•synononym:[Pfuscher],[Stümper]

^ü*Druse*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German drüese,alongside from Middle High German druose,from Middle High German druos,from Old High German tswelling,swollen gland. The gender and stem form of the Old High German are uncertain. It was probably a masculine,so the later forms in ''-e'' continue plural forms. Alternatively (or additionally) it may have been a feminine ''i''-stem,in which case from Middle High German drüese continues the plural and oblique singular;  (whence the doublet from German notext1) would be a compromise form. Cognate with from Old Saxon thrōs. The word also exists in parts of West Central German (compare from Luxembourgish däischter),which probably facilitated the borrowing; but the standardised form is definitely from Low German in view of its lacking diphthongisation.|Pronunciation}/ˈdyːstər/+ˈdyːstɐ}^Ⓓ6/6f/De-^@.ogg}düs+ter; dü+ster+caption''before the 1996 reform''|Adjective}#dark,dim,gloomy,obscure}#figurative cheerless,melancholy,somber|Usage notes}The general word for “dark” is dunkel,which is usual in all contexts and refers to both light and colour. The words finster and ^@ are chiefly restricted to the sense “lacking light”; both of them often have an undertone of eeriness or somberness. In contemporary German,usually means a virtual lack of light,while  tends to mean a dim twilight.}The contracted comparative ''düstrer'' is per se rare,but more commonly seen in the inflected forms,e.g. ''düstrere,düstrerer'' (in order to avoid the three reduced syllables and reduplication in ''düst'''e'''rere,düst'''e'''rerer'').||German Low German{}|Alternative forms}@^|Etymology}From from Middle Low German dü̂ster,from from Old Saxon tdark. ^ä*Erdmannchen*German{}|Etymology}From Erde,(earth) ground,Männchen,(little man). The original sense is that of a gnome,though the word was also used metaphorically or jocularly for animals in some dialects,e.g. for the mole. The use for “meerkat” has only become established in scientific use since the 1960s,but is older in Namibian German,where it also referred to the similar-looking Cape ground squirrel (species). ^ü*erubrigen*German{}|Etymology}From er-,übrig,(remaining) left over,-en,hence “to leave over,have as surplus”. Accordingly,the reflexive  actually means “to be left,remain” and one would originally say  in the sense of “XY still remains to be done”. The quite opposite contemporary sense seems to emerge around 1900. It probably developed through confusion with the active verb in the sense of “to spare”. Moreover,that which is left to be done last is often the least important thing and may in fact become redundant through developments in the meantime.|Pronunciation}^Ⓓf/f6/De-^@.ogg|Verb}#können to leave over,have extra,put aside,spare}•Er hatte etwas Geld '''@-2t'''.}•He had '''put aside''' some money.}•Sie gab alles,was sie '''^@''' konnte.}•She gave all she could '''spare'''.}#reflexive to be or become gratuitous,redundant,no longer necessary}•Nach allem,was wir heute wissen,'''@-2t sich''' diese Frage.}•With all we know today this question '''has become redundant'''.}#archaic to be left,to remain to be done}•Abschließend '''@-2t sich''' noch,historische Beispiele für beide Fälle zu geben.}•In closing,it '''remains''' for us to give historic examples for both cases.

^ü*fuhlen*German{}|Etymology}From northern from Middle High German vüelen (generally spelt from Middle High German vulen),from Old High German fuolen,from Proto-West Germanic tto feel,which see for cognates.}Upper German dialects of from Middle High German - used enphinden instead. In Modern German,empfinden has been chiefly confined to higher register. Nevertheless many southern dialects still lack or avoid ,usually preferring cognates of spüren.|Pronunciation}/ˈfyːlən/}^Ⓓf/f6/De-^@.ogg}^Ⓓd/d6/De-^@2.ogg|Verb}#transitive to feel (a thing,sensation,emotion - a noun)}•synononym:[spüren],[empfinden]}•Ich '''@-1''' den Sonnenschein auf meinem Gesicht.}•I '''feel''' the sunshine on my face.}•Ich '''@-1''' reines Glück.}•I '''feel''' sheer happiness.}#reflexive to feel (somehow - an adjective)}•Ich '''@-1''' mich verschwitzt.}•I '''feel''' sweaty.}•Ich '''@-1''' mich glücklich.}•I '''feel''' happy.}#}• „Vielleicht bin ich sogar verrückt. ^ü*Gammelbrudern*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈɡaml̩ˌbʁyːdɐn/}^Ⓓ9/9f/De-^@.ogg}Gam+mel+brü+dern|Noun}#Form of [@-1]
^ä*Gamse*German{}|Alternative forms}Gams,Gamsbock}Gemse|Etymology}From Middle High German gemeze,from Old High German gamiza (form only attested in a 13th-century manuscript). The variant Gams is from Middle High German gamz m,f,n,from Old High German ⋆gamuz or from Old High German ⋆gamaz (probably a masculine or neuter). These forms can be derived from gm,from Latin gf,which also underlie most of the dialectal Romance forms in Switzerland and northern Italy,probably from an extinct Alpine language}(such as from Raetic - or from Ancient Ligurian -),eventually perhaps from Proto-Indo-European without horns,although this is speculative. ^ä*garen*German{}|Alternative forms}gähren qualifier:obsolete|Etymology}From Middle High German jesen,from Old High German jesan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆jesaną. Variants with dissimilative hardening ''j-'' → ''g-'' before front vowels occur since Middle High German. The internal ''-r-'' is from the past forms (as in verlieren,schlagen),in part perhaps also from the causative from Old High German tto make ferment,from Proto-Germanic ⋆jazjaną. These developments were reinforced by association with the originally unrelated gar. Related to Gischt,from English yeast.|Pronunciation}/ˈɡɛːrən/+ˈɡɛː.ʁən+ˈɡeː-+-ɐn+ˈɡɛ(ː)ɐ̯n}^Ⓓ3/3b/De-^@.ogg}gern|Verb}((^@(gor,gegoren,göre,auxiliary:haben,sein),))}#intransitive to ferment}•synononym:fermentieren}#figurative to be agitated; to seethe}•Seit der letzten Niederlage '''gärte''' es in der Mannschaft gewaltig.}•Since the last defeat has there been great agitation among the team.|Usage notes}In the literal sense,the past tense is now usually ,though  exists as an alternative. The past participle predominantly remains strong (). In the figurative sense,only weak forms are commonly used.

^ä*Gerat*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German consultation; equipment,from Old High German advice,consultation,derived from Old High German advice,council,whence modern German Rat. The semantic development can,theoretically,be explained internally through a path “consultation” → “precaution” → “equipment”. However,the word has without doubt been influenced by another term,at hand in from Old High German stuff,equipment,which is related with bereit. Both became homophonous in many Low and Central German dialects; compare from Middle Low German consultation; equipment,which can be cognate with either Old High German word. The Middle High German sources show that the sense “equipment” did indeed spread from the north. Cognate with from Swedish geråd. Compare from Dutch gerei and from Dutch gereedschap.|Pronunciation}/ɡəˈʁɛːt/+ɡəˈʁɛːt standard; used naturally in western Germany and Switzerland}/ɡəˈʁeːt/overall more common; chiefly northern and eastern regions}^Ⓓ/f/f0/De-at-^@.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}^Ⓓ3/39/De-^@.ogg}Rhymes:ɛːt}gerät|Noun}(neut.,plural:[^@(e)s])}#countable device,tool,appliance,machine}•Bitte schalten Sie Ihre elektronischen '''^@e''' aus.}•Please turn off your electronic '''devices'''.}•einwandfrei}•einwandfreie '''^@e'''.}•faultless '''devices'''.}#uncountable equipment,tools}#dated contents,furniture|Hyponyms}Abschussgerät}Arbeitsgerät}Atemgerät}Aufnahmegerät}Aufzeichnungsgerät}Beatmungsgerät}Befeuchtungsgerät}Behandlungsgerät}Belüftungsgerät}Empfangsgerät}Faxgerät}Fernsehgerät}Funkgerät}Glasgerät}Haushaltsgerät}Heizgerät}Kochgerät}Kopiergerät}Küchengerät}Kundengerät}Laborgerät}Ladegerät}Magnetbandgerät}Mustergerät}Radiogerät}Schwirrgerät}Sendegerät}Sportgerät}Telefongerät}Tonbandgerät}Verarbeitungsgerät}Verschlüsselungsgerät}Warngerät|Derived terms}gerätemäßig

^ü*Gluck*German{}|Alternative forms}Glük|Etymology}From Middle High German gelücke (12th century),at first along the Lower and Middle Rhine. Probably borrowed from Old Dutch ⋆gilukki as part of the Flemish knight culture; compare from Middle Dutch gelucke (1240),whence modern from Dutch geluk. (The fact that the word is attested in High German before Dutch must be disregarded in view of the minimal attestation of Old Dutch as a whole.) Further origin unknown. Theories include a relation with from Dutch tto close in the sense of “that which is concluded,determined”,or with from German tto succeed,which is not attested in Dutch,however.
